f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001.demand: Weigh how the Governor's constitutional role both enables and strains Centre–State cooperation, ending in a balanced verdict.
intro_angles: Define the Governor's dual role as constitutional head of the State and link to the Union (Articles 153–162).
Open with the idea of cooperative federalism as a working relationship, not only a division of powers.

body_points.why: Examiner expects the textual basis before evaluation.
body_points.evidence_type: Relevant constitutional articles on appointment, discretion and assent
sub_points: Appointment and tenure at pleasure of the President
Discretion in summoning, assent and reservation of Bills

body_points.point: Ways the office supports cooperative federalism
body_points.why: 'Critically' needs the positive side, not only criticism.
body_points.evidence_type: Instances of the Governor acting as a bridge in Centre–State communication

body_points.point: Friction points: delays in assent, government formation, reports under Article 356
body_points.why: Core of the contemporary debate the question points at.
body_points.evidence_type: Recent Supreme Court judgments on the Governor's assent to State Bills

body_points.point: Commission and judicial recommendations on the office
body_points.evidence_type: Recommendations of the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions
body_points.example: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India on the limits of Article 356

body_points.point: Reforms to align the office with cooperative federalism
body_points.why: Way forward is expected in a 15-marker.
body_points.evidence_type: Proposals on time-bound assent and consultation with the Chief Minister in appointment

examples: A recent State–Governor standoff over pending Bills (describe, do not name dates you are unsure of)
Inter-State Council as an alternative forum
conclusion_angles: The office is a constitutional necessity; its misuse, not its existence, strains federalism.
Codified conventions and time limits can restore the Governor as a bridge rather than a veto point.
pitfalls: Writing only criticism — 'critically examine' needs both sides.
Listing articles without linking them to cooperative federalism.
Quoting figures on Article 356 use without being sure of them.
f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001.sources_note: Constitutional provisions on the Governor, reports of the Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions, and recent Supreme Court judgments on assent.
uncertainty: Whether the examiner expects the 2023 judgment on assent specifically is unclear; the point is phrased as an evidence type.

f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002.demand: Two parts: the challenges groundwater depletion poses, and practical measures for sustainable management.
intro_angles: State India's dependence on groundwater for irrigation and drinking water, as a fact without figures.

body_points.point: Causes of depletion: over-extraction for irrigation, free or subsidised power, water-intensive cropping
body_points.evidence_type: Central Ground Water Board assessments of over-exploited blocks

body_points.point: Consequences: falling water tables, quality contamination, rural distress
body_points.evidence_type: Recent data on arsenic and fluoride contamination in groundwater

body_points.point: Governance gaps: groundwater as an easement right attached to land
body_points.evidence_type: Legal status of groundwater and model groundwater bills

body_points.point: Measures: demand-side (crop diversification, micro-irrigation, power pricing) and supply-side (recharge, watershed works)
body_points.evidence_type: Government schemes on participatory groundwater management

examples: A state-level success in community groundwater management
conclusion_angles: Treat groundwater as a common-pool resource governed by users, backed by pricing and law.
pitfalls: Only listing schemes without linking them to causes.
f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000002.sources_note: Central Ground Water Board reports, NITI Aayog material on water management.

f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003.demand: Define probity in governance, then show with illustrations how it can be strengthened in public service delivery.
intro_angles: Define probity as integrity and uprightness that goes beyond mere legality.

body_points.point: Meaning of probity and how it differs from legality and efficiency
body_points.why: First part asks 'what do you understand'.
body_points.thinker: Kautilya on the conduct of officials

body_points.point: Why probity matters for service delivery: trust, equity, reduced leakages
body_points.why: Links the concept to the second part.
body_points.evidence_type: Instances where lack of probity distorted delivery

body_points.point: Institutional measures: citizen charters, social audits, RTI, grievance redress
body_points.evidence_type: Examples of social audits in rural employment schemes

body_points.point: Individual measures: codes of conduct, ethics training, leading by example
body_points.why: Ethics paper values attitudinal change, not only systems.
body_points.evidence_type: Recommendations of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission on ethics in governance

body_points.point: Technology: e-governance and direct benefit transfer reducing discretion
body_points.why: Modern illustration the examiner will expect.

conclusion_angles: Probity is sustained by systems and by conscience together; neither alone suffices.
pitfalls: Defining probity only as absence of corruption.
f0000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000003.sources_note: Second ARC report on ethics in governance; standard GS4 ethics texts.
uncertainty: Directive combines 'what do you understand' and 'illustrate'; recorded as 'Explain and illustrate'.
